# Results {#sec-results}

The previous chapter described a method for evaluating whether survey questions measuring similar concepts can actually be harmonized: pair every source question with every ACS question sharing its subtopic, then have three independent AI models rate each pair's feasibility, with arbitration resolving disagreements. This chapter reports what that process found.

The CPS contains 211 questions and FoodAPS contains 462 questions across four questionnaire instruments. Not all of these entered the analysis. Only questions whose subtopic classifications overlapped with ACS were eligible for pairing — 157 unique CPS questions (74% of the survey) and 118 unique FoodAPS questions (26% of the survey). The difference reflects each survey's conceptual distance from ACS: CPS shares broad labor force and demographic territory, while FoodAPS is predominantly a specialized food acquisition instrument whose questions on shopping frequency, food storage, and meal preparation have no ACS counterpart. These raw question counts also overstate what any single respondent encounters, since both surveys use branching logic that routes respondents through different question paths based on their circumstances.

Each eligible question was paired with every ACS question sharing its subtopic, producing 1,030 CPS–ACS pairs and 568 FoodAPS–ACS pairs. Most of these pairs were expected to fail — a question about weekly earnings and a question about commute mode might share an "Economic" subtopic but measure entirely different things. The purpose of the broad search was to ensure no viable match was missed. @fig-harmonization-funnel summarizes the funnel from total survey questions through to harmonization results. Across both surveys, 142 unique questions are candidate bridge variables for expert review.

![Harmonization funnel: from total survey questions through ACS concept overlap to viable harmonization paths. Percentages show concept overlap as share of total survey and harmonization paths as share of paired questions.](figures/fig03_harmonization_funnel.pdf){#fig-harmonization-funnel width=100%}

@fig-harmonizable-by-topic breaks these 142 candidates down by Census topic area.

![Harmonizable questions by topic for CPS and FoodAPS. Economic questions dominate both surveys, reflecting ACS's detailed coverage of employment, earnings, and labor force participation.](figures/fig04_harmonizable_by_topic.pdf){#fig-harmonizable-by-topic width=100%}

Economic questions lead both surveys — CPS contributes 56 and FoodAPS contributes 36 bridge variable candidates in earnings, employment status, hours worked, and SNAP participation. Social questions harmonize at identical counts (11 each) despite different underlying content: CPS covers disability and veteran status while FoodAPS covers food security and school enrollment. Demographic questions show the widest gap: CPS at 19 versus FoodAPS at 8, reflecting CPS's broader demographic measurement scope. The 27 demographic bridge variables across both surveys — age, sex, race, citizenship, household composition — also represent an opportunity for question standardization: surveys asking the same demographic questions in the same way would simplify harmonization from a statistical exercise to a mechanical one.

The next chapter examines what these results mean in practice — which harmonization paths are straightforward, which require methodological investment, and what the barrier patterns reveal about the feasibility of broader cross-survey integration.
